units.title: 1 The American Civil War and Reconstruction, 1846-77

topics.title: 1.1 How and why did sectional divisions widen between 1846 and 1861?

outcomes.text: Explain how westward expansion and Manifest Destiny deepened the North-South split.
Describe the debate over the Mexican Cession lands and the Calhoun Doctrine on states' rights.
Explain the Compromise of 1850 and the Kansas-Nebraska Act with Bleeding Kansas.
Explain the Fugitive Slave Act and the reactions to it.
Explain reactions to Uncle Tom's Cabin and the formation of the Republican Party.
Explain the impact of the Dred Scott decision and the Lincoln-Douglas debates.
Explain John Brown and Harpers Ferry.
Describe radical abolitionism: Garrison, Douglass and the Liberty Party.
Describe radical proslavery groups such as the Fire-Eaters.
Explain the 1860 presidential election and the first wave of secession and Confederacy formation.
Explain reactions to Fort Sumter and the second wave of secession.

topics.title: 1.2 How far did the Civil War transform the lives of Americans?

outcomes.text: Describe changes in military strategy and key battles: Antietam, Gettysburg, Vicksburg, Atlanta.
Explain why the Union won: industry, manpower, infrastructure and leadership.
Describe the destruction of the South, human loss and the state of North and South in 1865.
Describe the daily experiences of Northern and Southern soldiers.
Describe African American soldiers' contributions and experiences.
Describe women's military roles: nurses, spies, camp workers and soldiers.
Describe Hispanic American contributions and indigenous peoples' roles, including the Cherokee split.
Explain race riots and racial tensions in the North and Southwest.
Explain the pressure to end slavery and Lincoln's motives for the Emancipation Proclamation.
Explain the effects of emancipation and life in contraband camps.
Explain class conflicts and resistance to conscription.
Explain bread riots, inflation and shortages in the South.
Explain changes in gender roles on the homefronts.

topics.title: 1.3 What were the aims of Reconstruction and how successful was it?

outcomes.text: Explain Congress's focus on the west: the Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act.
Compare Lincoln's and Johnson's approaches to Reconstruction.
Explain the Black Codes, Johnson's clash with Congress and his pardons of ex-Confederates.
Explain the Reconstruction Amendments.
Explain the Military Reconstruction Acts.
Explain the impeachment charges against Johnson.
Describe efforts to rebuild infrastructure and the economy.
Explain carpetbaggers, scalawags and the Freedmen's Bureau.
Explain African American political participation.
Explain sharecropping and convict leasing as limits on Black prosperity.
Explain Southern resistance: literacy tests, grandfather clauses, poll taxes and the Ku Klux Klan.
Explain the costs, economic instability and the Compromise of 1877.
Explain how the Supreme Court weakened Reconstruction.
Explain the memory of Reconstruction: the Lost Cause and Southern Myth.

units.title: 2 Indigenous Societies, European Colonization, and the Atlantic World, c.1400s-c.1800

topics.title: 2.1 How and why did indigenous peoples and Europeans impact each other in North America?

outcomes.text: Describe eastern and Great Lakes groups and their lifestyles.
Describe Great Basin, Plains and Southeast groups.
Describe Southwest and Pacific Coast groups.
Explain the Powhatan Chiefdoms and the formation of the Iroquois Confederacy.
Explain the Iroquois alliance with the British.
Explain Algonquin-speaking alliances with the French and Spanish.
Explain the Iroquois (Beaver) Wars and the Pequot War.
Explain Metacom's War and Bacon's Rebellion.
Explain the Pueblo Revolt.
Explain transculturation, such as horses and glass beads.
Explain loss of indigenous territory to European powers.
Explain the spread of disease among indigenous populations.

topics.title: 2.2 Why did distinct colonial societies and economies develop in North America?

outcomes.text: Explain European motivations: trade routes, resources, national power and religion.
Describe the role of early explorers.
Describe Spanish, French and British claims and settlements.
Compare political power, economies and race relations in British, French, Spanish and Dutch colonies.
Compare the demographics, economies and politics of the Northern, Middle and Southern British colonies.

topics.title: 2.3 How and why did the Atlantic World shape the British colonies in North America?

outcomes.text: Explain mercantilism and salutary neglect: the Navigation and Restraining Acts.
Explain the economic importance of Triangular Trade.
Explain Enlightenment ideas, print culture, the First Great Awakening and Anglicization.
Explain how plantation agriculture grew and its impacts.
Describe the African slave trade and the middle passage.
Explain the development of race-based chattel slavery.
Describe distinct enslaved communities such as Gullah Geechee and Maroons.
Describe daily life on plantations.
Explain resistance and rebellions such as the Stono Rebellion.

units.title: 3 The American Revolution and the Emergence of a New Nation, c.1765-c.1815

topics.title: 3.1 Why did the Patriots desire independence from Great Britain?

subtopics.title: After the French and Indian War

outcomes.text: Explain the land gains and the Proclamation Line of 1763.
Explain British finances and colonists' opinions of the British army.
Explain the end of salutary neglect and the 1764-65 laws including the Stamp Act.
Explain the Townshend Acts.
Explain the Tea Act, the Boston Tea Party and the Intolerable Acts.
Explain the First and Second Continental Congresses.
Explain Enlightenment ideas of natural rights and the social contract, including Locke.
Explain the developing American identity and Paine's Common Sense.
Explain the preamble and natural rights in the Declaration of Independence.
Explain the grievances and the declaration of independence from Britain.

topics.title: 3.2 How and why did different groups support the Patriots, 1776-83?

outcomes.text: Explain why African Americans took part in the war and the freedom it could bring.
Describe African American military roles and long-term treatment of veterans.
Explain women's roles: homespun, boycotts, nursing, Daughters of Liberty and Republican Motherhood.
Explain why Spain, France and the Netherlands joined the conflict against Britain.
Explain the benefits to the Patriots of foreign help.
Explain indigenous alliances, the division of the Iroquois Confederacy and indigenous war roles.
Explain the loss of indigenous lands after the peace settlement.

topics.title: 3.3 Why did political parties emerge, and how did they evolve?

outcomes.text: Explain the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
Explain the Annapolis and Constitutional Conventions.
Compare the Virginia and New Jersey Plans and the Great Compromise.
Explain debates over slavery: the Three-Fifths Compromise and Slave Trade Clause.
Explain the Federalist and Antifederalist debate over ratification and the Bill of Rights.
Describe the leadership of Hamilton and Jefferson.
Explain the Federalist Party's ideology and policies.
Explain the Democratic Republican Party's ideology and policies.

subtopics.title: Federalist Era and Age of Jefferson

outcomes.text: Explain the debate over liberty and order, the Whiskey Rebellion and the Alien and Sedition Acts.
Explain debates over reactions to the French Revolution.
Explain impressment and violations of neutrality.
Explain the Louisiana Purchase, the Marshall Court and the War of 1812.

topics.title: 4.1 How and why did politics change from 1820 to 1850?

outcomes.text: Explain the spread of white manhood suffrage.
Explain the exclusion of women and free African Americans from voting.
Explain new campaign tactics aimed at new voters.
Explain Jackson's policies: the Bank War, veto, patronage and the Nullification Crisis.
Explain Democrat and Whig debates on internal improvements, federal versus state power, tariffs and expansion.
Explain the roles of the Anti-Masonic, Liberty, Know-Nothing and Free Soil parties.

topics.title: 4.2 Why did reform movements emerge, and how successful were they?

outcomes.text: Explain the Second Great Awakening: new denominations and evangelical ideas.
Explain how camp meetings and revivals spread evangelical ideas.
Explain transcendentalism and the criticism of the Market Revolution.
Describe Emerson, Thoreau, Fuller and utopian experiments such as Brook Farm.
Explain growing women's activism and its links with other movements.
Explain women's aims for legal and political status.
Explain the demands for suffrage, Seneca Falls and the Declaration of Sentiments.
Explain the temperance movement and the American Temperance Union.

topics.title: 4.3 Why did the debate over slavery intensify?

outcomes.text: Explain the importance of African Americans and women to abolitionism.
Explain the influence of the Second Great Awakening on abolitionism.
Explain the role of newspapers and the autobiographies of formerly enslaved people.
Explain the significance of the possible expansion of slavery into new territories.
Explain abolitionist religious, philosophical and economic arguments.
Explain disagreements among abolitionists about methods.
Explain the proslavery arguments: Southern culture, economic importance, property rights and religion.

topics.title: 5.1 Why and how did the Market Revolution impact the US economy and society?

outcomes.text: Describe railways, roads and canals.
Explain regional differences in development.
Explain the role of cotton in regional, national and global economies.
Explain changes in ideas of self-sufficiency, women's work and living standards.
Explain the role of class differences.
Describe the origins of immigrants and the reasons for and impacts of western migration.
Explain urban problems, nativism and anti-immigrant laws.

topics.title: 5.2 Why did westward expansion impact US politics and culture?

outcomes.text: Explain debates over Florida, Texas and the Mexican-American War.
Explain the debate over the acquisition of Oregon.
Explain the balance of power in Congress and the Missouri Compromise.
Explain how Mexican War lands threatened the sectional balance.
Describe the challenges of the Oregon Trail and the Gold Rush climate.
Explain clashes between settlers and indigenous peoples.
Explain the treatment of Hispanic and Asian heritage people.

topics.title: 5.3 How and why did US expansionism impact indigenous peoples?

outcomes.text: Explain the causes and effects of the Seminole Wars and the Black Seminoles.
Explain the motives for the Indian Removal Act.
Explain the legal challenges and the Trail of Tears.
Explain federal policies including the Bureau of Indian Affairs and the 1851 Appropriations Act.
Explain the effects of the Homestead Act and the transcontinental railroad.
Explain the reservation system, Americanization and boarding schools.
Explain the Sand Creek Massacre and Red Cloud's War.
Explain the Red River War and the Great Sioux War.
